data.name: Tyr: Chains of Valhalla
data.detailed_description:
Tyr: Chains of Valhalla é inspirado na mitologia nórdica, mais precisamente, o Ragnarök! Em um mundo tecnológico em que a humanidade depende de megaempresas como a Yggdrasil, as grandes empresas não conhecem limites, competem pelo monopólio global e os inimigos estão na ordem do dia; alguém tem que colocar um equilíbrio na cidade.

Tyr, criação do Professor Oswald Din, também conhecido como O.Din, tem a missão de impedir que Lemuz Oki, também conhecido como L.Oki, destrua a ordem mundial e crie um novo reino de caos para conquistar a maior empresa de tecnologia, bem como controlar todo o processo. mundo. Tyr, com a ajuda de Huginn & Muninn ("pensamento" e "memória") e seu fiel Sleipnir, ele assumirá o ápice de Valhalla para deter os planos malignos de L.Oki e seu grupo de vikings e robots.

Em um universo ciberpunk nórdico, onde a luta entre grandes corporações destrói o mundo como o conhecemos, um herói deve trazer ordem neste mundo. Em Tyr: Chains of Valhalla você pode encontrar o clímax e o ímpeto do Ragnarök visto de uma perspectiva cyberpunk.

Tyr: Chains of Valhalla é um jogo de tiro / plataforma 2.5D cheio de power-ups, vikings, robôs, chefes incríveis e difíceis. Tyr: Chains of Valhalla combina cenários 3D e chefes com personagens 2D e inimigos.

O tempo está contra você! Então seja rápido, preciso e acima de tudo, poderoso! Liberte a cidade de Midgard nesta aventura épica através destes níveis incríveis e chegue à última missão ... Derrote todos os chefes de uma só vez!

reviews.review:
The difficulty in rating Tyr comes from the fact that it’s not all bad, it’s just not a good example of the game it wants to be. For every step it takes in the right direction there’s a misstep just around the corner, waiting to infuriate or induce tedium, sometimes both in equal measure. Rather than dwell on the negatives, what does Tyr do right?

Firstly, it’s apparent the music is pretty good. Strident and metallic, it does a good job of creating the heavy metal vibe any good shooter should have, maintaining energy and driving the player on. Whilst it doesn’t have very much in the way of variety or nuance, the sound track is certainly a notable high point. Sound effects are also acceptable, weapons sounding relatively meaty and traversal noise reflective of what your character is actually doing, be it wall sliding or jumping from one death to the next. Graphically, it’s more of a mixed bag. In game Tyr looks great, with colourful graphics and interesting sprites, each of the six stages looking different and representative of their differing environments. Enemy designs are generally good, although the bosses are somewhat underwhelming, and there’s a level of variety that goes beyond reuse of the same two or three enemies over and over. However, the story telling graphics, specifically the talking heads of your support team, Huginn and Muninn, are a tonal leap from the gritty heavy metal vibe that Tyr seems to be aiming at, and sometimes the storytelling slideshows are lacking some polish (although there’s very little plot to be found, and it’s more along the lines of “flavour text”).  Finally, because of the colour palette in some areas, moving obstacles can become quite difficult to see leading to unintentional deaths due to an inability to spot safe zones.

What might work the best is the elemental weakness system. In a rock-paper-scissors type mechanic Tyr’s opposition all have a particular vulnerability (fire, ice or plasma) and Tyr can cycle through these elements to select the most effective payload to whittle down the resistance. Whilst weaponry never seems to be ineffective irrespective of the current weapon selected, there is a definite and satisfying damage bonus to be had by matching your weapon to the weakness, handily displayed by a character next to the enemy’s health bar. There are also several power up’s available, retained until Tyr is damaged which include a rapid fire laser, grenades and triple shot. Several of the latter stage power ups are pleasingly vicious, and it’s pleasantly surprising not losing the weapon should Tyr be hit with the power up set on standby (Tyr can have 2 power ups in addition to his standard weapon, with cycling through the three identical to element cycling).

Tyr’s progress is also not hindered by his manoeuvrability and responsiveness. I’m led to believe that this has been improved from the initial release, but your main character generally controls well and has the capacity to double jump, wall climb and dash. However, the jump doesn’t feel well calibrated for some of the platforming sections making them more arduous than they have any right to be, and Tyr’s dash has a somewhat irritating cool down. Whilst there’s an upgrade system, the limited allocation of power up points and inability to redistribute them or earn more by replaying levels is also somewhat saddening. Tyr becomes very platforming intensive, especially in a couple of the later stages, and with some of those obstacles representing instant death (the moving “plasma” barriers are the most egregious example) it can become incredibly infuriating to repeat arduous sections over and over again. Some of this repetition is probably intentional difficulty, but because of the colour palette in some areas the moving obstacles can become quite difficult to see leading to unintentional deaths.

Because repeat sections you will, as Tyr’s level design relies strongly on foreknowledge. Without any form of camera control at all, losing life to unexpected electrified floors, plummeting to your doom and colliding with enemies wandering below your position are all common hazards. It’s difficult to pin down whether it’s incredibly poor level design or intentional, but it’s incredibly unsatisfying to begin a stage, drop down from your starting platform and immediately land on an unseen enemy.  In addition to not being able to see it, anything beyond the screen limits may as well not exist. Projectiles don’t travel beyond the borders and enemies are effectively deactivated you can’t shoot them and they can’t shoot you. Whilst this might be handy to fudge some difficult sections it makes no sense, and renders any sense of a connected world moot. Tyr’s boldest conceit, to limit the player to a mere sixty minutes to finish the game has dire implications on the gameplay, changing it from a shooter to a “dash through the level as fast as possible ignoring everything but the critical path” game.

 There’s no point destroying enemies, no benefit to exploration, and if you get delayed just restart...each second might be critical. And as a result the interesting combat mechanic gets relegated to a footnote. Combat just takes time that is better spent making progress through the relatively short levels. Speaking of the levels, sometimes the design and checkpointing is woeful. This is especially the case on later levels where there might be a difficult section of platforming near the end, or even beginning, of the stage, followed by a wave of enemies or one hit kill barriers. Because the stages are quite small this may have been deemed a necessity, but thanks to the time mechanic and the small health bar it quickly becomes infuriating. It feels like lazy level design to create challenge and sadly is somewhat disincentivising for the player.

Then there’s the myriad of other niggles. The translation is woeful, and the as hinted at previously the writing is tonally at odds with the heavy metal feel that game seems to be aiming for. The childish quips from Huginn and Muninn feel wrong, as does the somewhat ill-advised T-Boy nickname. Spelling errors abound, at this point both in the game itself and even on the achievement list, and the level layouts are not represented accurately. Stages with angled, sloping corners are merely a background feature, a visual conceit with wall and the floor meeting at a standard ninety degrees. Placed immediately prior to a section of dangerous wall jumping, something that might otherwise be overlooked is frustrating due to the critical importance of height for that section. This also highlights the terrible i-frame timing. There’s no tolerance for mistakes, and no leeway due to almost no grace period following damage. A single error often results in multiple hits or even premature death, making the platforming sections more difficult than they should be.

The bosses are also uninspiring and it’s unclear whether they have weaknesses. Unlike the standard enemies they have no health bar or vulnerability indicator, both of which would be useful in determination of progress. They’re also not very engaging in design or mechanics, although they are thankfully deemed as separate stages, a restart allowing a quick repetition without the necessity of travelling through the preceding level. Whilst they’re not quite unfair, in certain instances attack patterns allow no safe haven, which in a shooter isn’t quite acceptable (in fairness this only happened with the first boss Garm). The game is also horrendously optimised and the link to Norse mythology is tenuous at best. 

I wanted to like Tyr, imagining a challenging shooter, but with a time limit that encourages skipping through levels as quickly as possible and frustrating platforming sections, it’s hard to recommend a game that doesn’t make good on its initial promise. If you’re looking for a challenging shooter you’d be better off with something like RIVE or even Turrican 2. Not Recommended.
